## 1. The dataset

Do people steer an AI coding assistant differently at the start of a session than at the end? `human_long` is a bundled dataset in `Nestimate` containing the coded human turns of **429 human-AI coding sessions across 34 projects**. Every row is a single action taken during a session, with a `cluster` label grouping the nine action codes into three broad types: `Directive`, `Evaluative` and `Metacognitive`.

```{r load}
data(human_long, package = "Nestimate")
head(human_long)
```

## 2. Split by time — early vs late interactions

For each session, the first half of its actions is labeled `"early"` and the second half `"late"`. Base R `ave()` does both jobs — per-session count and per-session position — and then a single `ifelse()` writes the label.

```{r split}
dat <- human_long[order(human_long$session_id, human_long$order_in_session), ]
n_per <- ave(dat$order_in_session, dat$session_id, FUN = length)
pos   <- ave(dat$order_in_session, dat$session_id, FUN = seq_along)
dat$half <- ifelse(pos <= n_per %/% 2, "early", "late")
table(dat$half)
```

## 3. Build the grouped network

`build_network()` is the canonical entry point. Passing `group = "half"` produces a `netobject_group` with one netobject per half; each stores the session-half sequences that `sequence_compare()` counts patterns in.

```{r build}
net <- build_network(
  data   = dat,
  actor  = "session_id",
  action = "cluster",
  group  = "half",
  method = "relative"
)
net
```

## 4. Compare patterns between early and late

`sequence_compare()` accepts a `netobject_group` directly — group labels are read from the list names, no separate `group` argument needed. Pattern lengths 3–5 (the default `sub = 3:5`), minimum frequency 25, chi-square test with FDR correction (the default `adjust = "fdr"`).

```{r compare}
res <- sequence_compare(net, min_freq = 25L, test = "chisq")
res
```

`summary()` returns the full per-pattern table, one row per pattern, ranked by the test statistic:

```{r top-table}
head(summary(res), 10)
```

### How to read the residuals

For every pattern, the standardized residual is computed from a 2x2 contingency table `(this pattern vs. everything else)`:

$$\text{stdres}_{ij} = \frac{O_{ij} - E_{ij}}{\sqrt{E_{ij} \cdot (1 - r_i/N) \cdot (1 - c_j/N)}}$$

- **Positive on `early`** → over-represented in the first half of sessions
- **Positive on `late`** → over-represented in the second half
- `|z| > 1.96` corresponds to `p < 0.05`; `|z| > 3` is very strong evidence

## 5. Pyramid plot

Back-to-back bars with residual labels inside each segment. Both sides use the same standardized-residual color scale.

```{r pyramid}
plot(res, style = "pyramid", show_residuals = TRUE)
```

## 6. Heatmap

Same top patterns, same color scale, alternative layout. Works for any number of groups (pyramid requires exactly 2).

```{r heatmap}
plot(res, style = "heatmap")
```

## 7. Sort by frequency

By default patterns are ranked by test statistic. Pass `sort = "frequency"` to rank by total occurrence count instead — useful for focusing on the most common patterns regardless of their group difference.

```{r sort-freq}
plot(res, style = "pyramid", sort = "frequency", show_residuals = TRUE)
```


## 8. Note on the test choice

The split-within-session design makes the two halves of one session non-independent (same human, same AI, same project). `test = "permutation"` shuffles group labels at the sequence level and assumes the sequences are exchangeable, which paired halves are not, so it is not used here.

`test = "chisq"` answers the k-gram-level question "do the rates differ between halves?". It does not model the pairing either: every k-gram occurrence is treated as an independent count, so its p-values are best read as a ranking of the patterns that differ most, not as exact error rates. The permutation test is the right choice when the groups are independent cohorts (e.g., two projects), where each sequence belongs to one group only.
